citation.title: Adaptation to Visuomotor Rotations in Younger and Older Adults

study.eligibility_rationale: Upper-extremity visuomotor rotation task with younger vs older adult groups and both perturbation-phase and aftereffect measures, reported in English. "Practice with the visuomotor rotation of 75° CCW consisted of 10 blocks of 48 closed-loop trials each." and "For the open-loop posttest with cued absence of the visuomotor rotation, the posttest–pretest difference of final directions of hand movements was an aftereffect measure."
study.design_notes: Repeated exposure: the same participants of Experiment 1a served in Experiment 1b the next day — "Each participant of Experiment 1a performed Experiment 1b on the next day." Per dataset rule 1/2 only Experiment 1a is retained; Experiment 1b (75° CW, single target of 0°) is dropped as a repeated exposure of the same sample. Experiment 2 used a separate, independently recruited sample (19 younger, 18 older) with a 30° CCW rotation and a single practice target, so it forms a second, independent dataset. Context change check: within each retained experiment the adaptive-shift (rotation cued present) and aftereffect (rotation cued absent) open-loop tests use the same task, apparatus, hand and target set; only the cue colour of the start circle differs, so no contextual change between learning and aftereffect phases. Subgroup splits by explicit knowledge (Figures 3 and 5) and by mental-rotation score divide the same participants into smaller cells than the text's age groups — these are not independent contrasts and were not used as datasets. Ns: Experiment 1a reports 20 younger and 20 older analysed (ANOVA df F(1, 38)); excluded/lost participants are described as additional to these 40. Experiment 1a explicit-test analyses use F(1, 37) because "the file containing the results of the explicit tests of 1 older participant" was lost — this affects explicit shift, not the adaptive shift/aftereffect measures. Experiment 2 ANOVAs on adaptive shifts/aftereffects use F(4, 132), consistent with 19 + 18 participants and gender as an extra factor. Adaptation-phase means (initial direction errors) are printed in the text for Experiment 1a and Experiment 2; adaptive-shift and aftereffect group means appear only in figures.

outcomes.measure_name: Two candidate measures: (a) adaptive shift = posttest−pretest difference of final movement direction in the open-loop test with cued presence of the 75° rotation; (b) error of initial direction in the last block of closed-loop practice with the rotation
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: An adaptive shift of 75° would compensate the visuomotor rotation of 75°.
outcomes.operationalization: (a) Adaptive shift: for the visual open-loop posttest with cued presence of the visuomotor rotation, the posttest–pretest difference of the final direction of the hand movement, plotted separately for each of the eight target directions (Figure 2a); an ANOVA main effect of age was computed on these shifts averaged over target directions. (b) Initial direction error (direction after 200 ms of movement) in the tenth (last) of the 10 blocks of 48 closed-loop practice trials with the 75° CCW rotation, printed in the text for each age group. Both are negative-going measures in this experiment (75° CCW rotation), i.e. a more negative adaptive shift and a smaller residual initial-direction error indicate more adaptation.

outcomes.measure_ruling: measure: change_from_baseline. winner: The focus of the analyses of the test phase data is on the posttest–pretest differences of the final directions of hand movements. For the open-loop posttest with cued visuomotor rotation, the differences are designated as adaptive shifts. An adaptive shift of 75° would compensate the visuomotor rotation of 75°. The mean adaptive shifts are shown in Figure 2a, and they were stronger for the younger than for the older participants. | loser: Initial direction errors were 42.3° and 18.9° in the first and last block of practice for younger participants. For older participants, they were 53.6° and 27.7°. | The protocol asks for the adaptive change at the end of the initial perturbation exposure, with the perturbation still applied, preferring a block average of overall performance. The adaptive shift is exactly that: it is measured in the posttest phase in which the rotation was still in force and cued present ("Maintenance trials in the posttest phase were identical to practice trials with the visuomotor rotation"), it is a posttest−pretest difference (change from baseline) averaged over the eight target directions, it is the quantity the paper itself contrasts by age ("revealed only a significant main effect of age, F(1, 38)  5.7, p  .05"), and it is reported with dispersion ("For all means, standard errors are shown."). The competing measure, the initial direction error in the last closed-loop practice block, is a raw endpoint kinematic value printed without any dispersion and, in the parallel Experiment 2, is reported only pooled across age groups ("There was no difference between the two age groups"), so it cannot serve as the study's measure of overall adaptation. The third candidate location (the p5 ANOVA labelled baseline_corrected) reads the very same adaptive-shift quantity but prints only a bounded p, so it is kept on the record as a context/test statistic and not read for a value.

outcomes.measure_name: Aftereffect = posttest−pretest difference of final movement direction in the open-loop test with cued ABSENCE of the visuomotor rotation
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: There was only a small difference between the two age groups, with slightly stronger aftereffects of the older participants and a stronger aftereffect for oblique than for frontoparallel and sagittal directions.
outcomes.operationalization: Visual open-loop posttest in which the absence of the 75° CCW rotation was explicitly cued (green start circle), taken immediately after the practice phase and its cued-rotation open-loop test; the aftereffect is the posttest–pretest difference of final hand-movement direction, computed per target direction (8 directions) and averaged across them for the age comparison. In this experiment aftereffects are plotted as negative values, so a more negative value = a stronger aftereffect.

study.notes: The detected-item list missed the two genuine tables: Table 1 (page 3 of the PDF, "Comparison of the Age Groups of Experiments 1a and 1b on a Set of Control Variables") and Table 2 (page 9, "Comparison of the Age Groups of Experiment 2 on a Set of Control Variables"). Both report cognitive/sensorimotor screening variables (mental rotation, Digit Symbol, Vocabulary, motor battery) rather than adaptation or aftereffect outcomes, so neither carries protocol outcome numbers; Table 1's header "U (20, 20)" and Table 2's "U (19, 18)" do corroborate the analysed group sizes. Adaptive shift and aftereffect group means are never printed numerically in the text for the age-group contrasts; they appear only in Figures 2, 4 and 6, so the second pass will have limited numeric material beyond the reported F statistics and the practice-phase initial direction errors. An extinction phase in Experiment 1a is mentioned but not reported: "For the sake of brevity, the findings of this phase are not reported..." Footnote 3 reports a supplementary combined analysis of Experiments 1b and 2 (76 participants) by explicit knowledge, which mixes samples and sign-flips Experiment 1b data; not usable as a dataset.
